This resource will serve to empower the next generation of Drosophila research and provides an important road map for similar efforts in other groups of organisms.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Highly contiguous assemblies of 101 drosophilid genomes" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Patricia Wittkopp as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Timothy B Sackton (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

The reviewers and we appreciated the impressive community resource that has been carefully brought together and that this acts as an important road map for other clade-wide sequencing efforts.

The strong points of consensus that emerge across the reviews, and in the discussion with the reviewers, were:

1) The need for base accuracy to be incorporated into the quality metrics discussed.

2) The need to place the work into a broad context of large-scale genome efforts to expand the readership outside of Drosophila researchers and show the expanding wave of community efforts focused on high-quality reference genomes. Suggestions included the vertebrate genome project and the earth biogenome project.

3) The reviewers all noted that acknowledgement of previous work in Drosophilidae was lacking. Drosophila researches have clearly been leading this charge for a while and it would be good to place the current effort into prior work more thoroughly.

4) While annotation of these genomes is beyond the scope of the current paper, it would be good to include more of a discussion of the planned road map for annotation going forward.

These points all should be addressed in a revised version. Below we have copied each review in its entirety. The reviewers have read each other's reviews and agree that all of the points are reasonable. Please provide a point by point response to the reviews, with a focus on the above broad goals.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

– Data availability. I found all (or at least most) of the raw sequencing data. I couldn't find assembly accessions.

– Guidance for future sequencing work

A back of the envelope calculation based on typical core prices for PacBio Sequel II CLR sequencing and Illumina Novaseq PE150 reads suggest a price total price of $14.50 / GB (< $2,175 / 150GB) and $9 / GB (< $6,750 / 750 GB) respectively. To sample a 150MB genome at 100-fold depth (15GB) for both platforms would seem to imply a cost of ~$350 (comparable to the price cited by the authors) or less. Accepting lower depth would lead to concomittant decreases in price / genome. The average sequencing depth for this project appears from Table S1 to be 9.8GB for long reads and 12.8GB for short reads, implying that the PacBio approach might be a bit cheaper. I don't think a detailed price analysis is necessary (or even advisable), but communicating the fact that the authors' approach is one of at least two more or less equally viable approaches would be both valuable and accurate.

– Quality control metrics: sequencing error and sample polymorphism

A description of the consensus error rate of the assemblies would be an important piece of documentation serving two purposes. It permits users to quantify the amount of error they might expect from this particular resource. Relatedly, since many of these samples are conducted on strains for which near isogenic samples are difficult to acquire, measuring and reporting the heterozygosity would help guide users as to the extent of this property of the material from which the assembly was derived, especially if such users intend to use the reference strains described here for conducting genetic work.

– Context via comparison to existing resources

Existing resources for highly contiguous assemblies (operatively, contig N50 > 1MB)

– The total number of existing assemblies is already at least 75 with N50 >= 1MB (57 from NCBI[1], 13 from Miller[2], 4 from Comeault[3], 1 from Rezvykh[4]).

– Obviously, this includes a lot of within-species samples (especially for D. melanogaster, including many assemblies of the reference strain) and many assemblies that have been subsequently improved by the authors. However, the authors are also sampling the same species multiple times (including the D. melanogaster reference strain) to their total count, so this is at least consistent with their counting.

– Importantly, this resource triples unique species possessing highly contiguous assemblies from 34 to 102 and expands species group representation from 8 to 15. Although, the quinaria group, represented by D. innubila, already existed and wasn't sampled again here, they re-sample 7 of the previous 8 species groups and add 7 more.

– As far as I can tell, until now, the most distant relative of D. melanogaster within Drosophilidae with a highly contiguous genome was Scaptodrosophila lebanonensis, which is in the tribe Colocasiomyini. The manuscript adds two additional members of this tribe, Leucophenga varia and Chymomyza costata. So, the number of distant relatives is tripled, but the actual phylogenetic breadth isn't (if my understanding of Drosophilid taxonomy is correct, and it may not be)

Scholarship

The $1,000 Nanopore genome was cited by both [2] and [5].

"Future work to improve biological and taxonomic diversity, particularly for species difficult to culture, should employ single fly sequencing and assembly workflows (Adams et al., 2020)."

An earlier long read precedent can be found in [6].

In addition to enumerating other high-quality Drosophila genomes that already exist, it would be extremely useful to users to see a comparison of the quality of the resources when they have published descriptions (in order to guide authors as to what types of contiguity, completeness, and error they can expect, especially in comparison to this work). At the least, I think the authors should put their work in the context of best previous assemblies for each species (an operative definition of contig N50 > 1 Mb seems consistent with their own thinking), particularly when that work has been published. To be consistent with their own accounting, they might even consider addressing works like [7], and species that have experienced extensive high quality sequencing effort like D. obscura, D. simulans, and D. pseudoobscura. I have attached a table with entries corresponding to every species in Table S2 as well as additional species exceeding contig N50 of 1Mb, including citations and NCBI accession numbers when they could be found.

The authors have actually cited many of these assemblies in other work [8], including genomes that have yet to be published, so it would seem that the authors are aware of them and trust the quality enough to incorporate into their own work, so improving the scholarship should be straightforward.

Typo

– In the abstract. There are 93 species represented, not 95.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

While this manuscript presents a large amount of valuable new data, and is inherently important for that reason alone, I believe that some key improvements and additional analyses could greatly strengthen this manuscript and really improve the value to the community.

1) Improvements to quality metrics.

This paper reports genomes that are at the low-cost end of the cost/quality tradeoff in genome assembly. This is a extremely valuable contribution, because many other large-scale projects in genomics (most notably, the Vertebrate Genome Project) have focused on the other end of this spectrum. Yet, for many researchers, a low-cost way to produce 10 genomes from related species may be higher value than a "complete" assembly from one species. However, it remains somewhat unclear exactly how good these genomes are, beyond the observation that the gene space is largely complete, and contig N50s are generally high.

Therefore, I think the biggest and most important improvement that would increase the reach and usefulness of this manuscript is improvements to quality metrics. A recent preprint from the Vertebrate Genome Project team (Rhie et al., 2020; https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.05.22.110833v1.full) provides a number of potentially useful quality metrics that may be worth considering applying here, although of course not all will be relevant to this project, and I realize the computational burden of trying to do everything could be large. Nonetheless, I think it is crucial to be able to give some sense of consensus quality, as base-level errors in assemblies has negative effects on many downstream applications. Based on Koren et al., 2019, there appears to be a large drop in likelihood of disrupting a gene due to a indel error between QV30 and QV40, and Rhie et al., 2020 has a lot more detail on various aspects of consensus quality metrics. I realize that many existing tools, e.g. Merqury (also Rhie et al., 2020, in Genome Biology) make the assumption that Illumina data is available for the same individual as the genome assembly, which is not universally true here (even in approximation, e.g. treating a strain as an individual). Still, some attempt to tackle this problem seems necessary, even if it cannot be done perfectly.

2) Assembly content

Related to the first point, basic descriptions of genome size (e.g., estimated from k-mers) would help to contextualize the resource produced, as would a definition of "near chromosome level contiguity" and validation of which of the newly reported assemblies here reach that threshold (especially as contig N50s vary by several orders of magnitude). Again, I don't think the VGP definitions are the only possible way to approach this question, but there is value in having some systematic summary of overall contiguity.

This paper does not describe the extent to which heterogametic sex chromosomes (not expected in all species based on sampling) or mitochondrial genomes are recovered. Presumably at least the presence of mt scaffolds is picked up in the NCBI screens, and is the kind of information that would be relatively straightforward to add to a table.

3) Drosophila focus.

There is a tension throughout this manuscript between describing a basically Drosophila-specific resource, and describing a more generally applicable approach to low-cost, clade-wide assembly. I think that the latter is really necessary and important, since not every community or group has the resources (in money, samples, compute) or desire (for their scientific questions) to use a "VGP-style" approach (with long reads, short reads, HiC, and optical mapping to produce as close to error-free chromosomal assemblies as possible). But the value of this manuscript as a blueprint for low-cost community genomics is somewhat limited by the Drosophila-centric nature of the results.

The most obvious Drosophila-specific assumptions are the availability of a inbred strain, and a genome size of 100-250 Mb or so, with a few exceptions. Notably, the assemblies of the larger genomes (and the ones derived from wild-caught flies) tend to be worse, with lower contig N50s and auN metrics, more contigs, and more fragmented or missing BUSCOs.

Of course it would be well beyond the scope of this manuscript to attempt to validate any of these approaches in other clades, or provide a simple recipe for how to assembly any possible genome. Nonetheless, it would certainly be possible to broaden the discussion, and be clearer in the text when certain statements are Drosophila specific (e.g., the $350 in sequencing costs assumes a genome on the order of 100-200 Mb).

4) Limitations of the existing resource and future prospects for improvement:

The genomes presented here do not include annotations, or any other form of supplemental resource such as whole genome alignments (e.g. Armstrong et al., 2020), and don't use HiC or any kind of scaffolding to obtain true chromosomal scaffolds. I think these are understandable and defensible choices, given the computational and technical requirements to extend this work in those directions. However, it may be valuable to discuss more explicitly what this resource is and is not. At a minimum, doing so could prevent the corresponding authors from receiving many emails asking where the gene annotations for species X are once this work is published.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

This is really an impressive resource and has the potential to be widely used both in terms of the data itself and also the methodology. I have several suggestions that may improve the manuscript.

There are several species (willistoni, paulistorum, etc.) that are sequenced more than once without any reference to why. It might be useful to describe that somewhere (Table 1?). As a resource, it would be simpler to use if it was clear when one isolate per species vs. multiple were appropriate to use for analyses.

Lines 59-61 – a bit more detail about modifications here since you are writing methods last.

Lines 107-111 – I'm concerned about the conclusions drawn about repeat content based upon the way the data was analyzed. A comprehensive analysis of repeat content is probably beyond the scope of this manuscript, but without de novo characterization of repeat sequences, I'm worried that satellites and TEs in more distantly related species may be missed if they are lineage restricted. I believe TRF would get at this to a point, but maybe not robustly. Other software like RepeatModeler might be better. However, my suggestion is not that these genomes are individually de novo annotated for repeats. It is just that the conclusions about relationships between contiguity or genome size and repeat content are presented with more caveats.

Figure 2 – This figure is a bit difficult to intuit, so this is another place where more detail in the main text would be useful.

Figure 3 – though the authors argue that this tree is not meant as a robust measure of phylogenetic relationships, it would be nice to put some support values on the tree.

Line 336 – I think the bioawk people would appreciate a citation (though all I can find on the internet is to cite the github page).

Line 340 – Please describe the auN statistic (what is L and what are we summing over?) in more detail. The Li github page describes nicely.

claims.claim: GenomeScope was used to estimate genome size from Illumina reads using a k-mer counting approach.
claims.source: To estimate genome size from Illumina reads, we used the k-mer counting approach implemented in GenomeScope v1.0.0 (Vurture et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for genome size estimation from short reads.

claims.claim: Regions annotated as single-copy BUSCO genes were used to estimate genome size from long reads.
claims.source: Since the higher error rate of Nanopore reads (5–15%) precludes the use of k-mer based reference-free approaches for genome size estimation, we instead used regions annotated as a single-copy BUSCO gene to estimate genome size.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for genome size estimation from long reads.

claims.claim: The higher error rate of Nanopore reads (5–15%) precludes the use of k-mer based reference-free approaches for genome size estimation.
claims.source: Since the higher error rate of Nanopore reads (5–15%) precludes the use of k-mer based reference-free approaches for genome size estimation, we instead used regions annotated as a single-copy BUSCO gene to estimate genome size.
claims.evidence: This is a rationale for the chosen methodology.

claims.claim: Flye produced significantly more contiguous assemblies than those reported by Miller et al. 2018.
claims.source: In addition to a much shorter (8–12 hr wall-clock time) runtime, Flye also produced significantly more contiguous assemblies than those reported by Miller et al. (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of assembly methods.

claims.claim: Canu produced relatively contiguous assemblies but a single assembly took several days on a 92-core cloud server.
claims.source: Canu produced relatively contiguous assemblies, but a single assembly took several days on a 92-core cloud server and even longer when a large number of extra-long (>50kb) reads were present in the data.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the computational requirements of Canu.

claims.claim: Haplotig identification and removal was performed if the BUSCO duplication rate exceeded 1%.
claims.source: If the BUSCO duplication rate exceeded 1%, haplotig identification and removal was performed, but on the draft assembly produced by Flye rather than the polished assembly.
claims.evidence: This describes a conditional step in the assembly pipeline.

claims.claim: Allowing Pilon to fix gaps or local misassemblies in default mode introduced large spurious indels in regions where short reads map poorly.
claims.source: We found that allowing Pilon to fix gaps or local misassemblies in default mode introduced large spurious indels in regions where short reads map poorly such as tandem repeats.
claims.evidence: This is an observation about the behavior of Pilon.

claims.claim: Spurious indels introduced by Pilon were not supported by long reads or by comparison to a reference assembly.
claims.source: These variants were not supported by long reads or by comparison to a reference assembly.
claims.evidence: This is evidence that the indels were errors.

claims.claim: BLAST was used to remove any contigs not associated with at least one BUSCO that were also of bacterial, protozoan, or fungal origin.
claims.source: We used BLAST v2.10.0 (Altschul et al., 1990) to remove any contigs not associated with at least one BUSCO that were also of bacterial, protozoan, or fungal origin.
claims.evidence: This describes the decontamination procedure.

claims.claim: Any sequences flagged by the NCBI Contamination Screen were excluded or trimmed.
claims.source: Finally, any sequences flagged by the NCBI Contamination Screen were excluded or trimmed.
claims.evidence: This describes the decontamination procedure.

claims.claim: Each draft assembly was soft repeat masked with RepeatMasker at medium sensitivity.
claims.source: Each draft assembly was soft repeat masked with RepeatMasker v4.1.0 (Smit et al., 2013) at medium sensitivity, with both Dfam 3.1 (Hubley et al., 2016) and RepBase RepeatMasker edition (Bao et al., 2015) repeat libraries installed (options: --species Drosophila --xsmall).
claims.evidence: This describes the repeat masking procedure.

claims.claim: The auN statistic is the area under an Nx curve.
claims.source: The auN statistic (Li, 2020) is the area under an Nx curve, and can be computed by multiplying the length of each contig (Li) by the proportion of the assembled genome it accounts for (Li /∑Li), then summing these values for all i contigs
claims.evidence: This is a definition of a statistical measure.

claims.claim: auN is always sensitive to a break in the assembly.
claims.source: Contig N50 represents a single point on the Nx curve and may or may not be affected by assembly breaks, but auN is always sensitive to a break in the assembly.
claims.evidence: This is a property of the auN statistic.

claims.claim: auN is a fairer statistic for comparison between different versions of the same assembly than contig N50.
claims.source: Therefore, auN is a fairer statistic for comparison between different versions of the same assembly.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of auN.

claims.claim: BUSCO v3 was used during the assembly process for all assemblies.
claims.source: When this work was started, BUSCO v3 was the current version. Version 4 was released while the project was ongoing. For consistency, version three was used during the assembly process for all assemblies, but the completeness of all final assemblies was assessed with BUSCO v4.
claims.evidence: This describes the versioning of BUSCO used in the study.

claims.claim: The completeness of all final assemblies was assessed with BUSCO v4.
claims.source: When this work was started, BUSCO v3 was the current version. Version 4 was released while the project was ongoing. For consistency, version three was used during the assembly process for all assemblies, but the completeness of all final assemblies was assessed with BUSCO v4.
claims.evidence: This describes the versioning of BUSCO used in the study.

claims.claim: Variants were called with PEPPER-Margin-Deepvariant for long reads and BCFtools for short reads.
claims.source: Long and short reads (if available) were mapped separately to each finished genome and variant calling was performed with PEPPER-Margin-DeepVariant (Shafin et al., 2021) for long reads and BCFtools (Danecek et al., 2021; Li, 2011) for short reads.
claims.evidence: This describes the variant calling methodology.

claims.claim: Only sites with minimum read depth 10, site quality score 30, and genotype quality score 30 were kept for variant analysis.
claims.source: Only sites with minimum read depth 10, site quality score 30, and (if applicable) genotype quality score 30 filters were kept.
claims.evidence: This describes the quality filtering applied to variant calls.

claims.claim: Reference-free quality score estimates were computed with Merqury following the developer's instructions.
claims.source: Reference-free quality score estimates were computed with Merqury v1.3 (Rhie et al., 2020), following the instructions provided by the developer on the GitHub repository (https://github.com/marbl/merqury).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for reference-free quality assessment.

claims.claim: Reference-based quality score estimates were computed with ONT Pomoxis for assemblies where a well-annotated counterpart of the same species and strain was available through NCBI RefSeq.
claims.source: Reference-based quality score estimates were computed ONT Pomoxis v0.3.7 (https://github.com/nanoporetech/pomoxis) for assemblies where a well-annotated counterpart of not only the same species but the same strain was available through the NCBI RefSeq database.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for reference-based quality assessment.

claims.claim: Pomoxis aligns each Nanopore-based assembly to the reference genome and assesses differences in 100 kb windows.
claims.source: Then, we ran Pomoxis, which aligns each Nanopore-based assembly to the reference genome and assessed differences between the two genomes in 100 kb windows (option: -c 100000).
claims.evidence: This describes how Pomoxis was used for quality assessment.

claims.claim: Species relationships were inferred using complete and single-copy orthologs identified by BUSCO analysis.
claims.source: We inferred species relationships using complete and single-copy orthologs identified by the BUSCO analysis.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for phylogenetic inference.

claims.claim: 250 out of 990 single-copy orthologs present in all assemblies were randomly selected to construct gene trees.
claims.source: Out of 990 single-copy orthologs present in all assemblies, we randomly selected 250 to construct gene trees.
claims.evidence: This describes the sampling for phylogenetic inference.

claims.claim: Amino acid sequences were used instead of nucleotide sequences to achieve better alignments in the face of high-sequence divergence.
claims.source: Amino acid sequences were used instead of nucleotide sequences to achieve better alignments in the face of high-sequence divergence (Bininda-Emonds, 2005).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological choice with a cited rationale.

claims.claim: Gene trees were inferred with RAxML-NG using the Le and Gascuel, 2008 amino acid substitution model.
claims.source: Gene trees were inferred with RAxML-NG v0.9.0 (Kozlov et al., 2019), using the Le and Gascuel, 2008 amino acid substitution model (options: --msa-format FASTA --data-type AA --model LG).
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for gene tree inference.

claims.claim: ASTRAL-MP was used to reconstruct the species tree from gene trees.
claims.source: The summary method ASTRAL-MP v.5.14.7 (Yin et al., 2019) was run with default settings to reconstruct the species tree.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for species tree inference.

claims.claim: The phylogenetic reconstruction is not intended to be definitive.
claims.source: We note that this is not intended to be a definitive phylogenetic reconstruction of species relationships; see Suvorov et al., 2021 for a time-calibrated phylogeny utilizing 158 drosophilid whole genomes.
claims.evidence: This is a caveat about the scope of the phylogenetic analysis.

claims.claim: Phylogenetically independent contrasts were computed for the counts of bases in repetitive and non-repetitive categories.
claims.source: Phylogenetic independent contrasts (Felsenstein, 1985) were computed for the counts of bases in both categories using the R package ape v5.4.1 (Paradis and Schliep, 2019) using the species tree described above with the root age set to 53 million years following the estimate in Suvorov et al., 2021.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodology for analyzing repeat content and genome size.

claims.claim: Docker and Singularity were used to manage computing containers.
claims.source: Specifically, we used the programs Docker and Singularity to manage containers.
claims.evidence: This describes the computational infrastructure used.

claims.claim: A Dockerfile is a text file containing instructions to set up a Docker image.
claims.source: A Dockerfile, a text file containing instructions to set up an image, is used to select the Linux operating system and the suite of programs to be installed within a Docker container.
claims.evidence: This is a description of Docker functionality.

results.result: The study generated 101 highly contiguous and complete genome assemblies for 93 drosophilid species using Oxford Nanopore sequencing. The assemblies have an average contig N50 of 10.5 Mb, with 94 assemblies containing over 98% of sequence in contigs larger than 10 kb and N50s exceeding 1 Mb. BUSCO completeness exceeds 97% in 97/101 assemblies.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C6, C22-C24, and C26 collectively demonstrate high assembly quality through multiple independent metrics (contiguity, completeness, correlation with genome size estimates). The quantitative measures are clearly stated and supported by the data presented in figures and supplementary files.

results.result: Nanopore-based assemblies are highly accurate in coding regions despite variable genome-wide quality scores. Manual validation of D. melanogaster revealed only 32 coding indels in 21 of 13,913 genes (0.15%), with most differences explained by poor short-read mapping in repetitive regions and supported by independent long-read assemblies.
results.evaluation: Claims C7 and C35-C51 provide converging evidence from reference-based quality assessment, manual curation, and comparison with independent assemblies. The detailed characterization of coding sequence accuracy, including the finding that errors cluster in specific genomic regions and that large insertions are often supported by other long-read assemblies, strongly supports the conclusion that coding regions are highly accurate.

results.result: The modified Nanopore sequencing protocol enables cost-effective genome assembly at approximately $350 per Drosophila line, with optimal runs yielding 12-15 Gb per flow cell at >30× coverage with read N50 >20 kb and 30% of reads >50 kb.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C20-C21, and C62-C64 describe the practical outcomes of the modified protocol. The cost estimate and sequencing metrics are based on empirical data from the study. However, these represent optimal conditions and actual results varied with sample quality (as noted in the text).

results.result: Sample heterozygosity varied widely across assemblies (0.00035-1.1% from long reads, 0.0015-2.1% from short reads), with long-read estimates systematically lower than short-read estimates. No significant relationship was observed between heterozygosity and assembly contiguity.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 present quantitative measures of sample diversity with clear statistical support (p=0.30 for lack of correlation with contiguity). The systematic bias between long and short read estimates is acknowledged and the heterozygous variants consistently exceeded homozygous variants as expected.

results.result: Genome-wide quality scores varied substantially across assemblies, with estimates from short reads (QV17-QV45), long reads (QV19-QV52), and Merqury (QV16-QV40). Merqury estimates were on average higher but correlated with variant-calling based estimates.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 report quality score estimates from multiple independent methods with stated correlations (Spearman's ρ=0.642 and 0.684, p<2.2e-16). The consistency across methods and acknowledgment of factors affecting quality (strain differences, sample diversity) support these findings.

results.result: BUSCO-based synteny analysis revealed that single-copy orthologs cluster into six major groups corresponding to D. melanogaster chromosome arms, consistent with conserved Muller element gene content but extensive within-element shuffling across drosophilids.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 describe a synteny analysis that recapitulates known patterns of drosophilid chromosome evolution (cited as C65-C66). The graph-based visualization (Figure 4) clearly shows the expected clustering pattern, and the interpretation is consistent with established knowledge.

results.result: No correlation exists between assembly contiguity and repeat content, suggesting long-read sequencing overcomes challenges posed by repetitive sequences. A positive relationship between repetitive and non-repetitive sequence sizes suggests both contribute to genome size variation.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 present statistical findings from repeat analysis. The lack of correlation between contiguity and repeat content (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and positive relationship between repetitive and non-repetitive sequences (Spearman's ρ=0.679, p<2.2e-16, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) using phylogenetically independent contrasts support these conclusions.

results.result: Flye was selected as the assembler based on superior contiguity and favorable runtimes (8-12 hours) compared to Miniasm and Canu, with Flye producing significantly more contiguous assemblies than previously reported methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C71-C72 describe the assembler benchmarking with supporting data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2. The comparison shows clear differences in contiguity and runtime, justifying the choice of Flye. The authors appropriately note that assembler performance should be re-evaluated with current versions.

results.result: High contiguity (N50>20 Mb) can be achieved with minimal coverage (15-20×) of moderately long Nanopore reads (N50 ~27.5 kb), as demonstrated by downsampling analysis of D. jambulina.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 are supported by the downsampling experiment shown in Figure 6. The analysis demonstrates that near-chromosome-scale assemblies are achievable at lower coverage than used for most assemblies, though this is based on a single species and may not generalize to all samples.

results.result: Of 76 representative drosophilid genomes previously available on NCBI, only 25 have an N50 greater than 1 Mb, compared to 94 of 101 assemblies in this study exceeding this threshold.
results.evaluation: Claim C25 provides a direct comparison to existing resources using cited data (Hotaling et al., 2021) and is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1. This demonstrates the improvement in assembly quality achieved by this study.

results.result: Genome size was estimated separately from Nanopore and Illumina data, using GenomeScope for short reads and BUSCO coverage for long reads, with the latter approach necessitated by the 5-15% error rate of Nanopore reads precluding k-mer-based methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70 describe the genome size estimation methodology with clear rationale for the different approaches. The correlation between assembly size and estimated genome size (C24, Figure 1—figure supplement 4) validates the approach, though the authors acknowledge limitations of the long-read method.

results.result: Haplotig removal was performed when BUSCO duplication exceeded 1%. Pilon in default mode introduced spurious indels in regions with poor short-read mapping that were not supported by long reads or reference comparisons.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 describe quality control steps in the assembly pipeline. The observation about Pilon introducing spurious indels is supported by comparison to long reads and reference assemblies, leading to the modified approach of using Pilon only for SNV and indel correction (not gap filling).

results.result: The manuscript provides historical context for Drosophila genomics, noting that while high-quality assemblies exist for some species, they represent only a small fraction of the 1600+ described drosophilid species.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C10-C14 provide background information supported by citations and general knowledge. These claims establish the motivation for the study and are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: The sequenced samples represent substantial taxonomic, geographic, and ecological diversity, including 99 assemblies from 14 species groups in Drosophilinae, species from multiple continents and latitudes, and two independent transitions to leaf-mining herbivory.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C19 describe the sample composition with details provided in Table 1 and Supplementary files. The taxonomic and geographic diversity is clearly documented, though the claim about independent transitions to herbivory (C19) relies on established knowledge rather than new analysis.

results.result: Assembly decontamination was performed using BLAST to remove non-BUSCO contigs of microbial origin and NCBI Contamination Screen, followed by soft repeat masking with RepeatMasker using Dfam and RepBase libraries.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 describe standard quality control and annotation procedures that are clearly documented in the methods. These are routine bioinformatics steps appropriately applied to the assemblies.

results.result: The auN statistic (area under Nx curve) is always sensitive to assembly breaks and is a fairer metric than contig N50 for comparing different versions of the same assembly.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 describe a statistical measure with cited definition (Li, 2020). The properties of auN are mathematically sound and the rationale for its use is appropriate, though the claim that it is 'fairer' (C81) is somewhat subjective.

results.result: BUSCO v3 was used during assembly for consistency, while BUSCO v4 was used to assess completeness of all final assemblies.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 document the versioning of BUSCO used in the study. This is a straightforward methodological detail that is clearly stated and appropriate given the timeline of the project.

results.result: Variant calling was performed with PEPPER-Margin-DeepVariant for long reads and BCFtools for short reads, with quality filtering (depth ≥10, quality ≥30). Quality assessment used Merqury (reference-free) and Pomoxis (reference-based in 100 kb windows).
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 describe the variant calling and quality assessment methodology. These are standard approaches appropriately applied, with clear documentation of parameters and tools used.

results.result: Species relationships were inferred from 250 randomly selected single-copy BUSCO orthologs using amino acid sequences, with gene trees built by RAxML-NG and species tree by ASTRAL-MP. The authors note this is not intended as a definitive phylogeny.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C94 describe the phylogenetic analysis methodology with appropriate caveats (C94). The approach is standard and the authors appropriately reference a more comprehensive phylogenetic study (Suvorov et al., 2021) for definitive relationships.

results.result: Phylogenetically independent contrasts were computed for repetitive and non-repetitive sequence content using the species tree with root age set to 53 million years.
results.evaluation: Claim C95 describes the statistical method for analyzing repeat content evolution. The approach is appropriate for comparative analysis and the root age is taken from a cited comprehensive study (Suvorov et al., 2021).

results.result: Docker and Singularity were used to manage computing containers to ensure reproducibility across different computing environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C97 describe the computational infrastructure used for reproducibility. This is a methodological detail that is clearly documented and represents good practice for computational reproducibility.

results.result: The cost of a highly contiguous and complete Drosophila assembly based on long-read sequencing was previously estimated at about $1,000 USD.
results.evaluation: Claim C8 cites previous work (Miller et al., 2018; Solares et al., 2018) for this cost estimate. This is appropriately attributed background information used to contextualize the cost improvements achieved in this study.

results.result: Gene ordering in drosophilid Muller elements has been extensively shuffled over ~53 million years of evolution, but gene content of each element remains largely conserved.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C66 cite established knowledge about drosophilid genome evolution from multiple sources. This background information is well-supported by the cited literature and provides context for the synteny analysis.
